title: End compute with the work—not after an arbitrary idle gap
goal: Choose job-scoped or inactivity-scoped compute lifecycle from arrival gaps, startup tolerance, and cost evidence.
tag: Certification cycle 2 · focused lesson 2 · compute lifecycle and performance
concept:
A taxi hired for one trip stops charging when the trip ends. A rented room stays open until its idle timer expires. Those are different lifecycle boundaries.

Job-scoped compute follows the unit of work. Inactivity-scoped compute follows time since the last command. A short timeout can repeatedly stop and restart between predictable queries; a long timeout can pay for unused capacity. The right setting comes from observed gaps and startup tolerance, not a universal number.
example: Four reports arrive 90 seconds apart. A 60-second inactivity timeout suspends between every report, causing four starts. A 300-second timeout keeps one warehouse session alive for the burst. After the burst, job-scoped compute can terminate with the job; an inactivity timer waits for its threshold.

use_case.when: Use explicit compute-lifecycle design for scheduled bursts, sparse orchestration, and shared task graphs.
use_case.example: A retail platform runs four quarter-hour reconciliation queries, then remains idle for hours.
use_case.decision: Measure arrival gaps, queue/startup delay, idle cost, minimum billing, and workload support. Prefer work-scoped managed compute when supported; tune inactivity only where the platform exposes that boundary.

practice: Switch the toy burst between 60- and 300-second idle thresholds. Predict starts and idle seconds.
boundary: The local model treats startup as instant and counts only idle seconds. It omits DBUs/credits, 60-second minimum billing, query runtime, caches, autoscaling, queueing, cloud capacity, editions, permissions, and real vendor execution.

product_sections.title: Snowflake: AUTO_SUSPEND follows inactivity, not task completion
product_sections.html:
First-minute product recall: Complete the scheduled product refresher above.

-- Not executed in SnowflakeCREATE OR REPLACE WAREHOUSE REPORTING_WH  WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'SMALL'  AUTO_SUSPEND = 300  AUTO_RESUME = TRUE;

For a standard virtual warehouse, AUTO_SUSPEND is seconds of inactivity and defaults to 600; 0 or NULL means never suspend. The background suspension check runs about every 30 seconds, so it is not a precision timer. Snowflake advises matching the threshold to real workload gaps: repeated 2–3 minute gaps with a 1–2 minute timeout can create repeated resumes and minimum credit usage. Auto-resume reduces manual work but can add provisioning delay and may conflict with cost-access controls.

title: A Phaser waits for registered parties—departing tasks must deregister
goal: Coordinate changing Java worker groups without leaving a reusable barrier waiting for a task that has exited.
concept:
A hiking group counts who is still on the trail before leaving each checkpoint. If one hiker goes home but remains on the count sheet, everyone waits forever.

A Java Phaser is a reusable barrier with a party count that can change. arriveAndAwaitAdvance() reaches the checkpoint and waits. A task that will not join later phases should call arriveAndDeregister(); this records arrival now and reduces the party count for future phases.
example: Workers A, B, and C register for phase 0. C finishes permanently and deregisters. Phase 1 then expects only A and B. If C merely arrives without deregistering, phase 1 still expects three parties and stalls.

use_case.when: Use Phaser when a batch has multiple reusable stages and the number of participating tasks can change.
use_case.example: Three Kafka partition scanners finish discovery; one empty partition exits while two continue validation and publish stages.
use_case.decision: Use CountDownLatch for a one-shot fixed count and CyclicBarrier for a fixed reusable group. Use Phaser only when dynamic registration is worth its lifecycle complexity.

practice: Toggle C between deregistering and merely arriving. Predict phase-1 unarrived parties.
boundary: The Java example is single-threaded state manipulation. It omits real blocking, exceptions, interruption, timeout recovery, forceTermination, tiering, pool starvation, and task identity bookkeeping.

'+(ok?'advances with 2':'waits for absent C')+'
';};phaserExit.onchange=paintPhaser;paintPhaser();

title: A two-way door needs a rollback window—not just a rollback story
goal: Delegate reversible decisions while making the actual point of irreversibility visible.
concept:
A hotel room key is reversible while checkout is still available. After the building is demolished, “we can go back” is only a sentence.

Two-way-door decisions deserve faster, lower-level ownership because they can be reversed with limited cost. But reversibility decays: data transforms, contracts, user behavior, and deleted infrastructure can close the return path. State the rollback trigger, owner, evidence, and last safe time before delegating.
example: A team moves consumers from topic v1 to v2. For 48 hours it dual-writes and verifies lag plus counts. Before hour 48, rollback is a routing change. After v1 retention is deleted, the decision becomes materially harder to reverse.

use_case.when: Use explicit rollback windows for platform migrations and experiments described as reversible.
use_case.example: An EKS service moves Kafka consumers to a new schema while the old topic and serializer remain available for 48 hours.
use_case.decision: Delegate the two-way door with a named trigger and deadline. Escalate or add preservation controls when the return path depends on expensive restoration, regulatory approval, or irreversible data loss.

practice: Move the decision clock from hour 24 to hour 60. Watch the rollback path change from routing to recovery project.
boundary: The model uses one deadline and binary evidence. Real reversibility depends on data retention, legal constraints, schema compatibility, user actions, state divergence, restoration tests, and organizational authority.

title: MCP sampling is an era-dependent compatibility path—not a new-server default
goal: Route legacy sampling deliberately and migrate modern MCP servers to direct model-provider calls without hiding credential ownership.
tag: GenAI engineering · harness engineering · MCP sampling migration
concept:
An old office intercom can still work during a transition, but a new building should not install it as the main phone system.

MCP sampling let a server ask the connected client's model for a completion. The 2026-07-28 protocol deprecated that path; current SDK guidance says new servers should call their model provider directly. Compatibility code still needs negotiated-version and capability checks. The migration also moves model credentials and usage governance to the server side.
example: Tool summarize60 receives a call. On a 2025-era connection with declared sampling capability, its compatibility path can request client sampling. On a 2026-07-28 connection, the new implementation calls the configured provider. The harness records which route owns model choice, credentials, cost, and policy.

use_case.when: Use explicit routing while a server must support older MCP clients during a deprecation window.
use_case.example: An internal summarization tool serves one legacy desktop host and one modern automation harness.
use_case.decision: Build new work on direct provider calls. Keep legacy sampling behind version and capability checks, an owner, telemetry, and a removal date; never silently copy a user's client credentials into the server.

practice: Toggle the negotiated protocol era and watch model and credential ownership move between host and server.
boundary: The model routes two strings. It does not implement MCP transport, MRTR input_required, provider authentication, quotas, data residency, approvals, timeouts, retries, capability negotiation, or model output validation.

title: Two timed precursors turn insulating boron nitride into a p-type monolayer
goal: Understand the reported BCN growth mechanism and separate wafer-scale material evidence from complete CMOS readiness.
tag: Technology breakthroughs · 2D semiconductors · research deep dive
concept:
Baking bread needs yeast, flour, and water to arrive in the right proportions at the right time. Dumping one ingredient early makes patches instead of a uniform loaf.

The reported boron carbon nitride process coordinates two molecular precursors so boron, carbon, and nitrogen reach the growth surface with better spatial and temporal balance. Carbon atoms and dimers mainly substitute at nitrogen sites in a continuous, locally distorted boron-nitride lattice. The paper reports a monolayer p-type semiconductor across a 2-inch wafer.
example: In the teaching model, matched precursor delivery produces four uniform wafer zones. A mismatched carbon pulse produces two carbon-rich zones. The real team characterized 224 transistors from three growth batches; the toy does not reproduce those measurements.

use_case.when: Study this work when assessing candidate p-type 2D materials for complementary or monolithic 3D electronics research.
use_case.example: A device-research roadmap needs a scalable p-channel material to pair with stronger n-type 2D candidates.
use_case.decision: Treat the paper as material and transistor-array evidence. Require complementary circuits, integration temperature, contacts, yield, long-term stability, variability, and manufacturing throughput before a product bet.

practice: Toggle precursor timing and inspect how the toy changes wafer uniformity. Then name evidence the model cannot supply.
boundary: This is a qualitative local model. It does not simulate CVD chemistry, dehydrogenation, crystal defects, band structure, the 1.90 eV gap, mobility, current, threshold voltage, yield, or manufacturing integration.

title: An artifact name identifies one immutable v4 upload—publish a new name for the next stage
goal: Pass build outputs across GitHub Actions jobs without pretending a later job can mutate an existing artifact.
tag: CI/CD & GitHub Actions · artifacts · immutable handoffs
concept:
A sealed evidence bag can be read later, but adding another item means creating a new sealed bag. Reusing the label does not turn the first bag into a workspace.

GitHub's upload-artifact@v4 treats an uploaded artifact as immutable. A downstream job downloads it, transforms the files, and uploads a new artifact name. Artifacts are handoff snapshots with retention—not a shared mutable directory or durable package registry.
example: The build job uploads orders-raw. The signing job downloads it and creates orders-signed. Uploading the transformed bytes again as orders-raw is the wrong mental model; the two names preserve provenance between stages.

use_case.when: Use workflow artifacts when later jobs need exact files from an earlier job or a human needs a bounded run output.
use_case.example: A Java build on Linux publishes a JAR, then a protected signing job downloads and signs the same bytes.
use_case.decision: Use distinct stage names and digests. Use a package registry or object store for durable distribution; use caches only for replaceable acceleration inputs.

practice: Switch the signing stage between a new artifact name and attempted overwrite. Predict whether provenance remains clear.
boundary: The model tracks names and digests only. It omits GitHub service calls, compression, permissions, retention policy, hidden files, attestations, storage quotas, cross-run tokens, and action-version pinning.

title: An additive response field is compatible only if consumers tolerate unknown fields
goal: Evolve JSON APIs by testing consumer behavior, not by assuming every schema addition is safe.
concept:
A restaurant can add a new side dish to the menu. A customer who ignores unfamiliar items is fine; a robot that rejects any unknown line stops ordering.

JSON Schema allows properties not named in properties by default. A consumer that sets additionalProperties: false chooses a closed response shape. Adding riskBand to a server response is additive for a tolerant reader but breaking for that closed validator.
example: Version 1 returns {id,total}. Version 1.1 adds riskBand. The tolerant mobile client reads id and total and ignores the new field. The closed generated validator rejects the same response until regenerated or its compatibility policy changes.

use_case.when: Use consumer-aware compatibility checks before adding response fields, enum values, or polymorphic variants.
use_case.example: An order API adds a fraud risk band used by new clients while old clients remain deployed for months.
use_case.decision: Prefer tolerant response readers and explicit contract tests. If important consumers are closed, coordinate regeneration, negotiate a version, or use a new media type/endpoint instead of declaring the change harmless.

practice: Toggle the client between tolerant and closed. Predict whether the same additive response validates.
boundary: The toy checks one unknown field. It omits request compatibility, enums, code generation, oneOf discriminators, media types, semantic changes, caches, rollout telemetry, and actual OpenAPI tooling.
